ROOT: Roots anchor a plant and take up water from the soil. They are below the stem, even when part of a root is visible above ground.
SEED: A seed contains the beginning of a new plant. A seed packet's planting instructions describe how to help it start growing.
LEAF: Leaves use light to help a plant make food. The flat blade and its veins are useful details to notice when identifying a leaf.
STEM: A stem supports leaves and flowers. It also connects the plant's growing parts with the roots below.
BULB: A bulb stores food for a plant underground. Tulips and daffodils grow from bulbs rather than from a packet of seed each spring.
SOIL: Soil is the material around garden roots. It contains more than loose mineral particles: air, water, and decaying material are also part of it.
WATER: Water is the same liquid whether it is in a drinking glass, a garden hose, or a cooking pot. The container changes the scene, not the substance.
POT: Pot can name a cooking vessel or a plant container. The surrounding clues tell you which everyday use is intended.
ROW: A row is a line of things side by side. Garden plants, theater seats, and letters in a puzzle can all be arranged in rows.
BLOOM: Bloom can mean an open flower or the act of flowering. In a flower clue, it does not mean a leafy bud that has not opened.
PETAL: Petals are the often colorful parts around a flower's center. Flower shapes and the number of petals vary between plants.
FRUIT: Everyday fruit dishes can mix several kinds of plant produce. The serving word is culinary and does not require a botanical classification.
RIPE: Ripe means ready to eat or harvest. Ripeness and color do not have exactly the same relationship in every kind of fruit.
PICK: Pick can mean choose or pluck. In a harvest setting, it usually means gathering something from the plant.
BASKET: A basket is made by weaving flexible material. Its open structure and carrying handle make it useful for collecting garden produce.
RIM: The rim is the edge around an opening. A flowerpot, glass, and bowl each have a rim, but not all rims are the same shape.
FLOWER: A flower is the blossom, rather than the whole plant. In everyday speech, the word can also describe a plant grown for its blooms.
BRANCH: A branch is a woody limb extending from a tree or shrub. A twig is usually a smaller, thinner piece of that growth.
TREE: Trees have woody trunks and branches. Familiar garden trees may provide fruit, flowers, or shade, sometimes all three.
BARK: Bark is a tree's protective outer covering. Its color and texture can help distinguish one kind of tree from another.
SUN: The Sun is a star. Its closeness makes it look much larger and brighter than the points of light seen at night.
SHADE: Shade blocks direct sunlight. A shaded garden corner still receives some light; it is different from a completely dark room.
WHITE: White is a color description, not a flower or bird name. Crossings can help when a clue asks for a color rather than a species.
GREEN: Green describes many growing leaves. It is also a color name in its own right, so read whether the clue asks for a plant or its appearance.
COLOR: Color names such as red, blue, and yellow describe appearance. They can help with a flower scene without requiring botanical vocabulary.
CUT: Cut is an action, unlike a tool name such as scissors or knife. Matching the clue's part of speech helps narrow the answer.
SCENT: Scent means a smell, often a pleasant one. Flower scents vary, and not every colorful bloom has a strong fragrance.
DRY: Dry can be an adjective or an action. It can describe laundry after airing or what happens when moisture leaves a flower bundle.
SHED: A shed is a small storage building. In a garden scene, it may hold tools and supplies rather than livestock.
HANDLE: A handle is the part made for the hand to grip. Its shape depends on whether the object is carried, pulled, poured, or turned.
WOOD: Wood comes from trees and has a grain. Following that grain when sanding usually leaves a smoother surface.
SOFT: Soft describes something that yields to touch. It can refer to cloth, an animal's fur, or food that is easy to bite.
HANG: Hang means support something from above. A hook, cord, or branch can hold the weight while the object hangs below.
BIRD: Birds have feathers, beaks, and wings. Not every bird flies, so feathers are a more dependable identifying feature than flight alone.
WING: A bird's wing is covered with feathers. Insects have wings too, but their structure and covering are different.
BEAK: Beak and bill are two everyday names for a bird's hard mouthpart. Its shape often reflects how the bird gathers food.
FEATHER: Feathers help birds with warmth and, in many species, flight. Small soft down feathers have a different job from long wing feathers.
NEST: A nest is a place for eggs and young. Many birds build nests, but the materials and locations differ from one species to another.
TAIL: An animal's tail is behind the main part of its body. Tails can help with balance, movement, or signaling, depending on the animal.
FUR: Fur is hair covering an animal. It differs from a bird's feathers, even when both look soft and keep the animal warm.
PAW: Paw names the foot of an animal such as a cat, fox, or rabbit. A cow or horse instead has a hoof.
HOOF: A hoof is a hard covering on an animal's foot. Cattle, sheep, and goats have split hooves, while a horse's hoof is not split in two.
EAR: Ears receive sound. In an animal clue, the word usually asks for a body part rather than a call or other sound.
GRASS: Grass commonly covers lawns and meadows. A pasture is land where animals graze on grass and other low plants.
FENCE: A fence marks a boundary or encloses an area. The gate is its movable entrance rather than another name for the whole barrier.
GATE: A gate opens through a fence or other boundary. Hinges let it move, and a latch holds it closed.
BARN: A barn is a farm building. Its uses can include sheltering animals and storing hay, equipment, or crops.
SHEEP: Sheep are farm animals valued for wool and other products. A lamb is a young sheep, and an ewe is an adult female.
HAY: Hay is cut vegetation dried for animal feed. Straw is mainly the dry stalks left after a grain crop is harvested.
POND: A pond is a small body of still water. A creek or brook flows along a channel instead.
BANK: In a water scene, bank means the ground beside a river or creek. In a money scene, it names a financial business.
FISH: Fish live in water and breathe through gills. A seal or otter swims too, but it is a mammal rather than a fish.
ROCK: Rock is natural solid material. Pebble usually means a small piece, especially one rounded by moving water.
SHORE: Shore is land at the edge of water. It can border a lake as well as the sea.
TIDE: Tides are the regular changes in sea level. A single breaking wave is a different movement of the water.
SAND: Sand consists of small loose grains. A pebble is much larger than an individual grain of sand.
SHELL: Shell means a hard outer covering. The same everyday word can describe the outside of an egg, nut, or crab.
NUT: In cooking, nut names foods such as almonds and walnuts. Botanical classifications are more detailed than this everyday food category.
SEEDLING: A seedling is a young plant grown from a seed. Its first leaves and small roots are already part of the new plant.
RAIN: Rain is liquid water falling from clouds. Snow and hail reach the ground in solid forms instead.
SKY: Sky describes the overhead view from the ground. Clouds, the Sun, the Moon, and stars can all appear in that view.
CLOUD: Clouds contain tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both. Their gray appearance does not mean the water itself is gray.
NIGHT: Night is the dark part of the daily cycle. Dusk is the fading-light period around the approach of night.
LIGHT: Light makes things visible. A lamp produces light, while a mirror mainly reflects light arriving from elsewhere.
WIND: Wind is moving air. Breeze is the everyday word for a relatively gentle wind.
INSECT: An adult insect has six legs. Spiders have eight, so a spider is not an insect.
LEG: Leg can name a body part or a furniture support. Read the clue's setting before choosing between those ordinary meanings.
FLOUR: Flour is ground grain used in baking. The fine powder is different from whole kernels even when both come from the same crop.
SUGAR: Sugar sweetens baking mixtures and drinks. Granulated sugar and powdered sugar have different textures despite sharing the same sweet ingredient.
BUTTER: Butter is made by churning cream. It adds flavor and fat to baked goods as well as serving as a spread.
MILK: Milk is a dairy liquid used in drinks and batters. Cream is the richer portion, with a higher fat content.
EGG: A hen's egg has a shell, white, and yolk. Recipes sometimes use only one inner part rather than the whole egg.
WHISK: A whisk's loops help mix liquids and beat in air. It works differently from a flat spatula used to lift or turn food.
BOWL: A bowl has raised curved sides. That shape helps hold liquid or contain a mixture while it is stirred.
PAN: Pan is a broad kitchen word. A frying pan is used on a stove, while a loaf pan holds dough or batter in the oven.
OVEN: An oven cooks with heat surrounding the food. That differs from the direct bottom heat under a pan on a stovetop.
STIR: Stir means move a utensil through a mixture. It combines ingredients without necessarily beating in much air.
SPOON: A spoon has a small bowl at one end. It can hold liquid, unlike the prongs of a fork.
FORK: A fork's prongs hold pieces of food. A garden fork is a larger tool sharing that pronged shape.
KNIFE: A knife cuts with a blade. In the kitchen, the board beneath the food supports the ingredient while it is sliced.
SLICE: A slice is a flat cut portion of food. Slice can also be the action of cutting food into those portions.
PEEL: Peel can name an outer covering or the action of removing it. Citrus rind and potato skin are familiar examples.
CRUST: Crust can mean a pie's pastry shell or a loaf's baked outer surface. Both are outer parts, but they are made differently.
BREAD: Bread can be a whole loaf or pieces shared at a meal. The feeding story counts loaves before describing the remaining pieces.
DOUGH: Dough is a thick unbaked mixture that can be shaped. A batter is generally loose enough to pour or spoon.
BAKE: Baking uses dry heat in an oven. Boiling instead cooks food in bubbling liquid.
CHEESE: Cheese is made from milk curds. Mild and sharp describe flavor rather than whether a cheese is cut into a block or slice.
RICE: Rice is a grain that absorbs water as it cooks. The word names the grain, not the pot or the cooking method.
PASTA: Pasta comes in many shapes. Spaghetti is long and thin, while macaroni is commonly sold as short tubes.
SOUP: Soup is served with its liquid. A broth can be part of a soup or served by itself.
BROTH: Broth is a savory cooking liquid. Noodles and vegetables can be added to turn a bowl of broth into a fuller soup.
POTATO: A potato grows underground. Its eyes are small buds from which a new plant can grow.
CARROT: The part of a carrot usually eaten is its root. The leafy green top grows above the soil.
ONION: An onion bulb has many layers. Its outer dry skin is removed before the inner layers are chopped for cooking.
TOMATO: Tomatoes are used like vegetables in savory cooking. Botanically, their seed-bearing fruits belong in the fruit category.
LEMON: Lemon juice is sour. Zest is the thin colored outer peel used for flavor, not the thick white layer beneath it.
SAUCE: A sauce adds moisture or flavor to another food. It can be smooth, chunky, hot, or cold.
SALT: Salt is a seasoning usually paired with pepper on the table. A pinch describes a small amount rather than a special kind of it.
SWEET: Sweet describes flavor, not temperature or texture. A food can be sweet and cold, or sweet and warm.
JUICE: Juice is liquid released from fruit or vegetables. Pulp is the soft plant material that may remain mixed into it.
APPLE: An apple has a peel, flesh, and a seed-bearing core. Cider is made by pressing apples for their juice.
PEACH: A peach has a fuzzy skin and a hard pit. A nectarine is a close relative with smooth skin.
CHERRY: A cherry has a hard pit inside. A stem attached outside is a different part of the fruit.
CINNAMON: Cinnamon comes from bark. It is sold in rolled sticks as well as ground into a fine powder.
CREAM: Cream is the rich part of milk. Whipping adds air, which is why whipped cream becomes fluffy.
CHILL: Chill means lower a food's temperature. It does not necessarily mean freeze it solid.
PLATE: A plate is flatter than a bowl. Its broad surface is useful for separate portions of a meal.
CUP: Cup can name a drinking vessel or a measuring amount. A recipe's measured cup is not simply any small mug.
JAR: A jar has a wide opening that makes spooning and filling easier. A bottle usually has a narrower neck.
LID: A lid is a removable cover. On a cooking pot it helps contain heat and steam; on a jar it closes the opening.
COOKIE: American English uses cookie for a small sweet baked treat. In Britain, many such treats are called biscuits.
PIE: A pie has a filling supported or enclosed by pastry. Not every pie has a top crust.
SANDWICH: A sandwich places a filling between pieces of bread. An open-faced version uses just one supporting slice.
TEA: Tea is made by steeping leaves in water. Herbal drinks are often called teas too, although the plants can be different.
COFFEE: Coffee is brewed from roasted beans. The familiar beans are actually seeds from the coffee plant's fruit.
ICE: Ice is solid water. It absorbs heat as it melts, which helps cool a drink.
GIFT: A gift is something given, rather than sold. A tag identifies the recipient; wrapping protects or decorates the present.
CARD: A greeting card combines a message with a small printed or handmade sheet. It is different from a bank card or playing card.
PAPER: Paper can be folded, cut, and written on. Card stock is heavier and stiffer, making it useful for tags and greeting cards.
PEN: A pen writes with ink. A pencil uses graphite, which can usually be removed with an eraser.
PENCIL: The writing core of a modern pencil is graphite, not metallic lead. Lead remains a traditional everyday name for it.
PHOTO: Photo is short for photograph. A caption or name label can preserve information that the image alone does not supply.
BOOK: A book has pages joined inside a cover. The title names the work; the author is the person who wrote it.
PAGE: A page is one side of a book's paper. A single physical leaf normally has two pages, front and back.
NAME: A name identifies a person or thing. In a family album, adding names helps later readers recognize the people pictured.
DATE: A date identifies a day, usually with a month and year. It can distinguish a photo's occasion from the day its note was written.
NOTE: A note is a short written message. It can be a reminder, a greeting, or a brief explanation attached to an object.
STAMP: A postage stamp pays for carrying mail. It is different from a rubber stamp that applies an ink impression.
LETTER: Letter can mean a written message or one alphabet character. An envelope clue points to the message sense.
ENVELOPE: An envelope encloses a letter. The destination goes on its front; the message stays inside.
BOX: A box is a container rather than its contents. In a hobby clue, a kit may come in a box but the two words are not interchangeable.
BAG: A bag is a flexible carrying container. A pocket is generally a smaller compartment attached to clothing or another bag.
COIN: A coin is a piece of money. Bible parables sometimes use coins to tell a story about loss, work, or generosity rather than modern U.S. denominations.
PRICE: Price is the amount asked for an item. Change is money returned after a customer pays more than that amount.
CLOCK: A clock shows time. The hour hand moves more slowly than the minute hand on a traditional clock face.
HOUR: An hour contains sixty minutes. A minute contains sixty seconds; these two relationships are easy to mix up.
CALENDAR: A calendar organizes dates into weeks and months. Months vary in length, so a month is not exactly four weeks.
DOOR: A door is the movable panel at an entrance. Hinges let it swing, while a latch or lock holds it closed.
WINDOW: A window admits light through glass. A screen is a mesh barrier that can keep insects out when the glass is open.
CHAIR: A chair is intended for one sitter. A bench or sofa generally provides room for more than one person.
TABLE: A table provides a raised flat surface. Chairs are the separate furniture used to sit beside it.
SHELF: A shelf is a horizontal storage surface. A drawer is a compartment that slides in and out.
CLOTH: Cloth means fabric. A cloth used for wiping is an object made from that material, not a different substance.
COTTON: Cotton is a plant fiber used in many washable household items. Wool instead comes from an animal's fleece.
WOOL: Wool comes from sheep. It can be spun into yarn and then knitted or woven into warm fabric.
YARN: Yarn is a continuous strand of fibers. A ball or skein is a way to package it, not a separate kind of stitch.
THREAD: Thread is usually finer than knitting yarn. It passes through a sewing needle's eye to form stitches.
NEEDLE: A sewing needle has a point and an eye. Knitting needles generally use pointed ends to form loops without threading an eye.
STITCH: A stitch is one unit of worked thread or yarn. Many stitches together form a seam, knitted row, or decorative pattern.
SEAM: A seam joins pieces of fabric. A hem finishes an edge instead of joining two separate pieces.
FOLD: Folding brings one part of a sheet over another. A crease is the line left by pressing that fold.
SCISSORS: Scissors use two blades moving past one another. Finger loops help control the opening and closing action.
GLUE: Glue bonds surfaces together as it sets. Tape holds them with an adhesive already attached to a strip.
PAINT: Paint leaves a colored coating on a surface. A stain usually allows more of wood's natural grain to remain visible.
BRUSH: A brush holds many bristles in one handle. Their width and stiffness affect the marks or cleaning action it makes.
FRAME: A frame surrounds and supports an image or object. The glass, backing, and outer border are separate parts of a picture frame.
RIBBON: A ribbon is a narrow fabric strip. A looped bow and a straight trailing tail are different parts of a tied ribbon decoration.
KNOT: A knot holds a cord by bending it through loops. It can join ends or stop a strand from sliding through a hole.
LOOP: A loop is a curved opening in string or ribbon. It need not be tied into a knot to have that shape.
BEAD: A bead has a hole for threading. A bracelet can repeat bead colors in a pattern or use different sizes for contrast.
PATTERN: A pattern is an arrangement that repeats. In sewing, the same word can also mean a template for cutting fabric pieces.
PIECE: A piece is one part of a whole. Matching shape, color, and edges helps a jigsaw piece fit its correct place.
CORNER: A corner is where two edges meet. In a jigsaw, a corner piece normally has two outer edges.
FAMILY: Family can include several generations and relatives by marriage. A family tree shows relationships rather than everyone's physical appearance.
HOUSE: A house is a building. Home is the place associated with living and belonging, which need not be a separate house.
ROAD: A road is a route for vehicles. A sidewalk or footpath provides a different part of the journey for people on foot.
CAR: A car carries people on roads. Its trunk holds luggage, while the passenger compartment holds the seats.
KEY: A door key is shaped to match a particular lock. A spare is another key kept for use if the main one is unavailable.
TOOL: A tool is an implement used to do a job. The clue may describe its action, such as cutting, turning, or gripping.
SCREW: A screw has a spiral thread. Turning it moves it into material; a nail is usually driven with a hammer instead.
SNOW: Snow falls as ice crystals or groups of crystals. It differs from liquid rain and the hard pellets of hail.
WARM: Warm is a relative temperature word. Something warm has more heat than a cool object but is not usually described as hot.
BLANKET: A blanket is a covering used for warmth. A quilt usually has several layers held together with stitching.
HAT: A hat covers the head. The brim projects outward, while the crown is the part above it.
COAT: A coat is an outer garment. Its lining is inside, while the collar and pockets are visible features outside.
SHOE: A shoe's sole is its bottom surface. The upper covers the foot, and the heel is the raised or rear part.
SOCK: A sock covers the foot inside a shoe. Its heel, toe, and cuff name different parts of the same garment.
GARDEN: A garden is an area cultivated for plants. A single bed or plot can be one part of a larger garden.
SWEETPEA: Sweet pea is an ornamental flower, not the edible garden pea. Its seeds and pods are not food.
MYRRH: Myrrh is a fragrant resin, one of the gifts named in Matthew's wise-men story. It is not another name for gold.
SCEPTER: A scepter is a ceremonial staff representing royal authority. In Esther's story, the extended golden scepter signals that she may approach.
RHUBARB: Rhubarb stalks are used in pies and other cooked dishes. The leaves are not eaten.
MOSES: Exodus follows Moses from a basket by the river to leadership of his people. The separate scenes describe different times in his life.
JOSEPH: Genesis tells of Jacob's son Joseph, his brothers, and the grain stored in Egypt. This is a different Joseph from Mary's husband in the Nativity story.
JOHN: The New Testament includes both John the Baptist and John the fisherman. The Jordan baptism scene uses the former; the fishing scene uses the latter.
MARY: Mary is named as Jesus' mother in the Gospels. A story's setting helps distinguish her from other women named Mary.
SHEPHERD: A shepherd tends a flock of sheep. The Bible uses both real shepherds in its stories and shepherd imagery in its teachings.
MANNA: In Exodus 16, manna is gathered as food in the wilderness. The story describes it as white and tasting like wafers made with honey.
ARK: In Noah's story, ark names the large boat. Other Bible passages use the same English word for a sacred chest, a different object.
TEMPLE: The Jerusalem temple is a worship setting in the Gospels. It is a building, not the side-of-the-head meaning of the same word.
TOMB: The Easter narratives describe a burial place whose entrance was blocked by a stone. The puzzle follows the named Gospel passages rather than later decorative customs.
PALM: Palm can mean a tree or the inside of a hand. In the entry-to-Jerusalem story, it is the tree whose branches are carried.
MUSTARD: Mustard names a plant as well as a condiment made from its seeds. The parable concerns the small seed and its growing plant.
ROBE: A robe is a loose outer garment. In a Bible story it is clothing, not a separate kind of blanket or tablecloth.
LAMP: A lamp provides light from a fuel or electrical source. Bible lamps used oil rather than a modern bulb.
OIL: Oil has different uses in different scenes. It can be a cooking ingredient, lamp fuel, or part of a story about caring for a traveler.
STAR: A star is a celestial light. Matthew's wise-men story uses a star as a sign leading the visitors, rather than as a modern Christmas-tree ornament.
DONKEY: A donkey is a long-eared working animal. Colt names a young animal in the Gospel's entry-to-Jerusalem scene.
WEDDING: A wedding is the celebration of a marriage. John's Cana story takes place at that celebration, with guests and serving jars.
RIVER: A river is flowing water in a channel. In the baptism scene, Jordan is the proper name of the river.
PEACE: Peace can describe calm instead of conflict or disturbance. In the storm story, the setting concerns wind and water becoming still.
FEAST: A feast is a large celebratory meal. The meal's role depends on its story, such as welcoming a guest or celebrating a return.
CROWN: A crown can be royal headwear or the upper part of a hat. A folded paper version is a familiar Christmas-cracker prize.
GARLAND: A garland is a long decorative strand. A wreath is normally a ring, so the two words describe different arrangements.
CHRISTMAS: Christmas customs vary between households. These scenes include ordinary decorations and sharing activities as well as clearly labeled Christian stories elsewhere.
EASTER: Colored eggs and chocolate rabbits are seasonal customs. The separately labeled Bible puzzles concern the Christian stories associated with the holiday.
THANKSGIVING: In the United States, Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November. Families differ in their meals and activities.
HALLOWEEN: The ghost, witch, and bat scenes are pretend seasonal decorations. They do not ask the reader to accept supernatural claims.
SPRING: Spring is the season between winter and summer. Weather and the exact timing of flowers vary by U.S. region.
SUMMER: Summer scenes use familiar warm-weather outings. Actual temperatures and traditions differ between regions and families.
FALL: Fall is the usual American word for autumn. Both name the season after summer and before winter.
WINTER: Winter is the cold season in much of the United States. Snow scenes are familiar examples rather than conditions experienced everywhere.
SONG: A song has words and a melody. In the familiar-title puzzles, ordinary definitions help even when a reader does not remember the recording.
FILM: Film can name a motion picture or the light-sensitive strip once used in cameras. A screen or projector clue points to the movie setting.
MUSIC: Music can be played by instruments or sung. A concert is an event at which music is performed, rather than the music itself.
SCHOOL: Schoolday memories differ by generation. Chalkboards and lunch pails are selected older settings, not experiences shared by every reader.
TOY: A toy is made for play. A miniature model can be a toy, a hobby project, or a display depending on its use.
RAINBOW: A rainbow appears when light interacts with water drops. Its curved colored bands are a light effect, not a solid object.
WISHBONE: The wishbone is a forked bone in a bird's chest. Pulling it for a wish is a custom rather than a promise of future luck.
CORNUCOPIA: Cornucopia means a horn-shaped container overflowing with produce. It is a harvest decoration rather than a particular kind of fruit.
